feedback.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25,$ traversed from the point $(-5,0)$ to the point $(0,-5)$ in the third quadrant?
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $5$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/2ec6f01ab00c17d4888dfefb37c2813139af9c412e99acd1a38680274b0f0ddd.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡t+25{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{25({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & ={e}^{5(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{e}^{5(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}\cdot 5\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{e}^{5(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
